items.title: PHP Discloses Three New Critical Vulnerabilities
items.description: TL;DR PHP disclosed three additional critical vulnerabilities, separate from the PHP2Shell issues covered in our October analysis. Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, or 8.2.36, as appropriate for your branch; check with your vendor for package availability or backported fixes. Inventory PHP deployments and confirm each has an owner and a patch path. For background on the earlier PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, read our October analysis . PHP2Shell reminded us that PHP powers a vast range of websites, applications, and products, often running behind the scenes in places organizations may not immediately think to look. With three new advisories now drawing attention to PHP’s internals, security teams face a familiar challenge: understanding where the runtime is deployed, how it is configured, and who can move quickly when a fix is available.

items.title: 'November2Shell' Continues with 7 Patched Ruby Vulnerabilities
items.description: TL;DR Ruby fixed seven vulnerabilities in string case conversion and regular expression handling, with proof-of-concept exploits showing that some can lead to remote code execution. Organizations should upgrade to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10 and check vendor updates for Ruby bundled with applications or container images. Ruby has released security updates for seven vulnerabilities in its string case-conversion and regular-expression code. One of the flaws, known as Ruby2Shell ( CVE-2026-132825 ), can cause a heap buffer overflow when Ruby changes the case of a crafted string. The other vulnerabilities affect regular-expression compilation, matching, and conversion.

items.title: Optimizely Attack Shows Why Supply Chain Ownership Matters
items.description: TL;DR Malicious JavaScript added to Optimizely projects reached sites across multiple industries, including technology, finance, retail, and media. The injected JavaScript could swap cryptocurrency addresses, capture payment card information entered into website forms, collect some browser-accessible data, and attempt to deliver iOS exploit chains. Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and secured affected accounts. Organizations using Optimizely should review project code and account access, investigate relevant logs, and assess potential exposure based on how their sites handled payment and session data. The Optimizely incident shows how a change in one shared service can reach many organizations through software they already trust. On November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of websites using Optimizely Web Experimenta tion. Report URI identified 18 8 infected snippets across 178 organizations, including major technology, media, retail, financial services, and travel companies. A Shared Service Became a Shared Risk Optimizely lets customers add custom JavaScript to their projects. In this incident, malicious code was placed in a project's custom-code field. The altered snippet was then delivered as part of the site's normal Optimizely integration, so the change did not have to pass through each customer's source repository or software build. An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. Optimize ly fixed the vulnerability , rem oved the injected code, secured affected accounts, and added protections against unauthorized code delivery. This was not a case of attackers changing a customer's application source code or poisoning the CDN cache. The code was added to project settings and delivered as part of a service those websites relied on. An organization can secure its own code and infrastructure while still depending on external services that influence what reaches users. The Payload Turned Shared Dependence Into Shared Exposure The injected code used a loader to bring additional JavaScript into the page. Resear chers observed multiple loader versions , incl uding one that obscured the external address and another that carried an inline fallback. That meant blocking one destination alone might not remove every way the code could run. The payload combined several behaviors: Cryptocurrency address swapping : The script could replace cryptocurrency addresses in page content and during copy actions, potentially redirecting transfers. Transactions to attacker-controlled wallets were confirmed. Payment-card skimming : The code looked for card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes submitted through site-controlled forms. It could not access card fields inside cross-origin payment-provider iframes. The available reporting does not establish how many card details were captured. Browser data collection : The script could send page URLs, screenshots, and cookies available to JavaScript. Cookies marked HttpOnly are not available through document.cookie . iOS exploit delivery : On Apple mobile devices, the script attempted to load Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. Researchers have not established how many devices, if any, were successfully compromised. The confirmed cryptocurrency transactions show that at least one part of the operation had financial impact. These capabilities show why teams need to understand not only what code a service is expected to run, but also what that code can access and how changes to it are controlled. Integrity and Intelligence Must Cover the Full Path Component intelligence helps teams identify the software they use, understand its role, and assess its known risks. Artifact integrity addresses a different question: whether the software moving through development and delivery is still the expected artifact. Both matter because organizations need context about their components and confidence in what they build and distribute. The Optimizely incident exposes a gap between those controls and what happens in production. The malicious code was added through a third-party project setting and delivered to visitors' browsers. It did not need to enter a customer's source repository or change a locally built artifact. A package inventory or artifact check would not, by itself, show whether a vendor-managed script had changed. That doesn't make component intelligence or artifact integrity less relevant. It means organizations need to understand the scope of each control and account for the code paths it does not cover. Alongside knowing which components enter software and verifying the artifacts teams release, organizations need visibility into the external services that can change code running on their sites. Software Supply Chain Ownership Is an Operating Model Organizations using Optimizely Web should con sult Optimizely's incident update for current information and use their project and access records to determine whether their sites were affected. More broadly, this incident shows why responsibility for software inputs and services needs to be shared across development, platform, security, and web teams. Those teams need a common understanding of what their software depends on, how those dependencies reach production, and who is accountable for changes along the way. Owning the software supply chain means understanding what is being shipped and what external code can become part of the software customers use. Component intelligence, artifact integrity, and runtime visibility each help address a different part of that responsibility. For more on Sonatype's approach, check out our software supply chain security solution .

items.title: PolinRider Loader Reappears in Hijacked npm Packages
items.description: TL;DR Sonatype Research Labs identified concealed runtime loaders in 12 npm releases across 10 hijacked packages. All 12 releases contain loaders designed to decode payload-server IP addresses from Ethereum transactions sent by the same hard-coded wallet previously reported in PolinRider activity, then retrieve, XOR-decode, and execute JavaScript. Six conceal the loader in eval(atob(...)) ; six use a character-permutation bootstrap and the JavaScript  Function constructor. The manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. The code can run when an affected entrypoint is loaded or, for server-hemera-mongo, when the bundled application starts. Check direct and transitive dependencies, lockfiles, internal npm mirrors, and build records. If affected code ran, treat the host as compromised and investigate its processes, network activity, and accessible credentials. Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases across 10 hijacked packages. The examined releases contain two loader variants that use the same Ethereum sender wallet and payload-retrieval infrastructure. Sonatype tracks the finding as sonatype-2026-010515 . The affected packages support unrelated developer functions, from Redux integration and health APIs to browser activity tracking, utilities, and server examples. Their shared issue is concealed behavior embedded in code that otherwise serves those ordinary purposes. These releases don't rely on a consumer-side installation script to activate that behavior. An application can reach the code when it loads an affected package; the server-hemera-mongo releases run it as the service starts. Package Affected Releases Observed Behavior @adminide-stack/client-redux 0.0.16-18 Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64 @adminide-stack/health-api-server 0.0.18-alpha.465 Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64 @adminide-stack/user-activity-browser 1.1.3-alpha.114 Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64 @adminide-stack/utils 0.0.16-129, 0.0.16-130 Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64 in 0.0.16-129 and a character-permutation bootstrap in 0.0.16-130 server-hemera-mongo 0.0.15, 0.0.16 Ethereum-based loader concealed by Base64 cdeops 13.5.31 Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap @adminide-stack/forms-core 5.1.9-alpha.3 Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser 12.0.194 Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap @cdmbase/wiki-browser 12.0.18-alpha.53 Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap @pubngo-stack/help-browser 12.0.23-alpha.3 Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap   The Shared Loader Uses Ethereum Transactions to Find Remote Code All 12 releases contain loaders designed to query public Ethereum RPC endpoints, with a Blockscout API fallback, to locate a transaction sent by the hard-coded wallet 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3 . The loader interprets the first four bytes of the transaction's recipient address as a primary IPv4 address and the next four as a secondary address. It retrieves XOR-encoded JavaScript from the primary address over plain HTTP on TCP port 443, using the paths /0x/cls and /0x/ls . After XOR-decoding the responses, the loader passes the JavaScript retrieved from /0x/cls to eval in the application process and to a detached node -i process through piped standard input. The JavaScript retrieved from /0x/ls is passed only to a detached node -i process. The child processes are unreferenced, allowing them to continue independently of the application process. The Ethereum wallet acts as a dead-drop resolver: the operator can advertise a new payload-server IP address by sending another transaction without updating the malicious packages. Blocking an individual server therefore does not disable the loader's ability to discover a replacement. Six Releases Conceal the Ethereum Loader With a Different Bootstrap Six releases use a character-permutation bootstrap designed to reconstruct and execute an Ethereum-based loader: @adminide-stack/utils@0.0.16-130, cdeops@13.5.31, @adminide-stack/forms-core@5.1.9-alpha.3, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser@12.0.194, @cdmbase/wiki-browser@12.0.18-alpha.53, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser@12.0.23-alpha.3. The decoded loader bodies recovered from these six releases are byte-identical. They differ from the loader in the six Base64-wrapped releases but use the same Ethereum wallet, retrieval paths, and XOR keys. In utils@0.0.16-130, an obfuscated routine follows the package's logger code. It permutes and decodes an embedded blob, obtains the JavaScript Function constructor indirectly, and executes the decoded content. In cdeops@13.5.31, an obfuscated bootstrap appears in client.js before the module's normal delegation to global.require('cdeops/client'). It decodes embedded content and executes it dynamically, then continues to the expected client delegation. The hidden execution is separate from the documented purpose of that shim. Shared Wallet and C2 Infrastructure Link the Releases to PolinRider Sonatype Research Labs independently decoded the loaders in all 12 releases and recovered the same hard-coded Ethereum sender wallet, 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3 . This exact wallet appears in GitGuardian's October 27, 2026 repo rt, " GhostAction Crosses Paths With PolinRider: Inside the October Escalation ," where it is identified as the Ethereum resolver used by PolinRider loaders found in compromised GitHub repositories. Those earlier loaders also retrieved stages from /0x/cls and /0x/ls on port 443, matching the retrieval paths and port in the npm samples. The connection extends to the payload-server infrastructure. Greenflagged's analysis of these npm releases dec oded transactions from that wallet and reported 95.135.181.151 as the advertised C2 address at its November 3 observation. GitGuardian had already listed the same IP on port 443 as a fallback C2 in a PolinRider persistence script. The exact wallet match, overlapping server infrastructure, and matching stage-retrieval paths support linking these malicious npm releases to previously documented PolinRider activity . This connection does not depend solely on similarities in obfuscation, and it does not definitively establish that PolinRider and GhostAction share an operator. The Malicious Code Doesn't Wait for an Install Hook The package manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. Execution occurs when the runtime reaches an injected JavaScript file. For example, require('cdeops/client') selects the affected client.js , while the package's ES module import maps to a separate client.mjs file. In server-hemera-mongo, the injection is in dist/main.js , the application bundle referenced by its start script. Assess exposure by correlating dependency records with execution evidence. Lockfiles identify resolved dependency versions, while cached artifacts and download logs help trace package acquisition. Build commands, application configuration, process telemetry, and runtime logs help establish whether an injected JavaScript file was executed. Disabling npm install scripts does not address code that runs during module loading or application startup. The relevant question is whether the affected package code ran in a developer environment, CI worker, build host, or deployed service. What Teams Should Do Now Organizations should take these steps to identify affected systems and limit further exposure: Find affected versions : Check direct and transitive dependencies, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, internal npm mirrors, caches, build records, and artifact metadata. Evaluate repository protections : Determine whether your repository manager or dependency firewall blocked these releases before they reached developers or build systems. Review download and policy logs to identify any deliveries, and ensure all eight versions are blocked from future use. Remove affected dependencies : Replace affected versions in projects and prevent internal mirrors and caches from serving them. Preserve copies needed for investigation, and use replacement versions that have been independently verified as clean. Determine whether the code ran : Check which entrypoint the application loaded and whether the runtime could execute the injected code. Correlate this with process and network activity. A lockfile entry does not prove the malicious code ran, and an import error does not prove it didn’t. The import may have failed after the injected code executed. Investigate affected hosts : If the code ran, treat the host as compromised. Look for detached node -i processes launched by another Node process with piped standard input, and plain HTTP requests to TCP port 443 using /0x/cls or /0x/ls . Payload requests carry a Sec-V header containing A10-npm_inject in the six Base64-wrapped releases, A10-II in utils@0.0.16-130, or A10-E in cdeops@13.5.31. Use these indicators alongside process ancestry, timestamps, and dependency records to identify affected systems. Assess access and rotate credentials : Identify the credentials and systems available to the affected process. Rotate credentials where exposure is possible, including publishing credentials, source repository access, cloud keys, and CI secrets. The operator can change the remotely served JavaScript without publishing another npm release. Use available process, network, build, and runtime records to determine what affected systems executed and which credentials and resources those processes could access. For ongoing details and response guidance, se e the Sonatype Security Event and Sonatype Guide research . Thanks to Sonatype Research Labs' Adam Reynolds for analysis of the affected npm releases and their PolinRider activity. Connect with Adam on LinkedIn .

items.title: Stop Chasing CVEs: Start Governing Software Dependencies
items.description: A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.
